title: New EU safeguards on steel imports from third countries
key_claim: From 1 July 2026 Regulation (EU) 2026/1384 replaces the 2019 safeguard, cutting duty-free quotas, raising the out-of-quota duty to 50%, allocating country-specific quotas on 2022-2024 shares, and requiring importers to evidence the country of melt and pour.
frame_summary: Presents the quota architecture as a technical, rules-based and WTO-consistent successor to the expired safeguard rather than as a new kind of trade instrument.
verbatim_quote: At the time of importation, importers of products subject to the quotas must submit adequate and verifiable evidence — such as a mill certificate — to demonstrate the country in which the raw steel or iron was initially produced in liquid form and subsequently cast to reach its first solid state (hereinafter, the "country of melt and pour").
verbatim_list: From 1 July, Regulation (EU) 2026/1384 of the European Parliament and of the Council establishes a new regulatory framework replacing the safeguard measure under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/159, which applied until 30 June 2026.
By 30 June 2027, the Commission will assess whether the scope should be extended to products made from steel or containing a significant amount of steel that are not currently included in Annex I.
notes: Primary official explainer for the EU instrument. Quote verified by hand against the live page on 19/08/2026 via WebFetch; the audit script cannot reach europa.eu through the sandbox proxy.

publisher: UK Department for Business and Trade
title: UK's steel trade measure from 1 July 2026
key_claim: From 1 July 2026 the UK cut tariff-free steel quota volumes by 51% against the previous safeguard and applies a 50% tariff above those levels, citing OECD projections that the gap between global steel capacity and demand reaches 721 million metric tonnes by 2027.
frame_summary: Argues the quota cut is a deliberate defensive alignment with the EU measure to stop diverted steel arriving in Britain instead, framing volume control as the necessary response to overcapacity.
verbatim_quote: From 1 July 2026, the government is limiting tariff-free steel imports, reducing overall quota volumes by 51% compared with the steel safeguard measure.
verbatim_list: Any imports above these levels will face a 50% tariff.
notes: Evidence that the quantitative instrument is being copied outside the EU. Quote verified by hand against the live page on 19/08/2026 via WebFetch.

title: Canada launches public consultations on the administration of tariff-rate quotas for certain steel imports
key_claim: Canada is consulting on how it administers steel tariff-rate quotas introduced in June 2025 to address trade diversion, currently run through shipment-specific permits issued first come, first served.
frame_summary: Frames quota administration as a standing, adjustable policy tool for managing diverted steel rather than as an emergency remedy, which makes the quantitative instrument a permanent fixture of Canadian trade policy.
verbatim_quote: Canada currently administers these quotas through shipment-specific permits issued on a first-come, first-served basis.
verbatim_list: The TRQs were introduced in June 2025 to address the risk of steel trade diversion into the Canadian market and impacts of non-market policies and practices that drive global excess capacity.
notes: Third jurisdiction running the same instrument. Quote verified by hand against the live page on 19/08/2026 via WebFetch.

title: OECD Steel Outlook 2026
key_claim: The OECD projects global steel excess capacity to keep growing through 2028 against sluggish demand, with competition distorted by subsidisation concentrated outside the OECD area.
frame_summary: Argues that persistent subsidy-driven excess capacity is the root cause and that only collective action on those distortions, rather than unilateral border measures, restores a level playing field.
notes: Cited for the direction of the overcapacity trend only; no figure is drawn from this page. The OECD site is JavaScript-rendered and the body text is not retrievable by the audit fetcher, so no verbatim quote is recorded.

title: Europe has had enough of China's export surge
key_claim: On European Commission estimates global steel overcapacity could reach 721 million tonnes by 2027, near five times EU consumption, while the EU cuts tariff-free quotas by 47 percent from roughly 33 million tonnes to 18.3 million and doubles out-of-quota duties to 50 percent through 2031.
frame_summary: Argues that Europe is moving past product-by-product tariffs toward quantity-based and industrial-policy instruments because tariffs alone cannot contain an economy-wide overcapacity shock.
verbatim_quote: Beginning in July 2026, the EU will cut tariff-free steel quotas by 47 percent, from roughly 33 million tonnes to 18.3 million, and will double out-of-quota duties from 25 percent to 50 percent through 2031.
verbatim_list: According to European Commission estimates, global steel overcapacity could reach 721 million tonnes by 2027—nearly five times total EU steel consumption.
notes: Quantification anchor for the quota volumes and the overcapacity backdrop. The 721 million tonne figure is attributed by this source to European Commission estimates, not to the OECD. Quotes verified by hand against the live page on 19/08/2026 via WebFetch.

title: Neues EU-Handelsschutzinstrument für Stahl startet
key_claim: The German steel association says the new ceiling is not rigid like the old safeguard but breathes with the market, and presses the Commission to close the remaining routes around it.
frame_summary: Argues that the volume instrument is the necessary and effective successor to the safeguard, and that the live risk is circumvention rather than over-protection.
verbatim_quote: Dabei ist die Obergrenze nicht starr wie bei den bisherigen EU-Safeguards, sondern „atmet“ mit der aktuellen Marktsituation.
verbatim_list: Mit dem heutigen Inkrafttreten des neuen EU-Handelsschutzinstruments für Stahl hat die Europäische Union Handlungsfähigkeit bewiesen: Ein wirkungsvolles Nachfolgeinstrument für die ausgelaufenen Safeguards ist damit etabliert.
notes: German-language primary-market source. Quote verified by hand against the live page on 19/08/2026 via WebFetch.

title: Steel, Still Standing: post-safeguard steel overcapacity measures in the EU and the United Kingdom
key_claim: Both the EU and UK measures were designed to sit outside the WTO Safeguards Agreement, but a panel could still treat them as a de facto continuation of the expired safeguards, which would hand exporters leverage to negotiate larger quotas.
frame_summary: Argues that the legal insulation of the new quota regimes is more fragile than their designers claim, so their permanence should not be assumed.
verbatim_quote: In the meantime, the possibility that a WTO panel could characterise either measure as a de facto continuation of the expired safeguards provides exporting countries with a source of negotiating leverage for increased TRQs.
verbatim_list: However, despite deliberately distancing themselves from safeguards, potential WTO challenges might arise from the de facto continuity between the old and new systems, given certain structural similarities.
notes: Counter-evidence: legal fragility of the instrument. Contributed by BLOMSTEIN. Quote verified by hand against the live page on 19/08/2026 via WebFetch.

title: Brazil criticizes new EU restrictions on steel
key_claim: Brazil's government states that no compensation agreement was reached with the EU under Article XXVIII of the GATT and warns the measure may trigger an escalation of trade defence measures.
frame_summary: Argues that restricting trade with suppliers who did not cause the oversupply solves nothing and invites retaliation, so the instrument is destabilising rather than corrective.
verbatim_quote: The government also reported that no agreement was reached with the European Union regarding compensation for the new tariffs, as stipulated in Article XXVIII of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT).
verbatim_list: The statement adds that restricting trade with countries that are not responsible for the global oversupply does not resolve the issue and may trigger an escalation of trade defense measures.
notes: Counter-evidence: affected-partner objection and retaliation risk. Quote verified by hand against the live page on 19/08/2026 via WebFetch.
